results.original_text: Milddail (Welsh); Achillea millefolium (Latin). Known in the medieval Welsh herbal tradition of the Meddygon Myddfai, Carmarthenshire, 13th century. results.translation: Yarrow [Milddail], known for its many-cleft leaves, was employed by the Physicians of Myddfai chiefly as a vulnerary [wound-healer], applied externally to stanch bleeding and close fresh cuts, and taken internally as a decoction to purge [cleanse] the blood of corrupt humours. It was likewise prescribed for fevers of an intermittent kind, and for griping [cramping] pains of the stomach and bowels, the plant being considered warm and dry in its virtue and therefore suitable for cold, moist distempers. An infusion of the leaves and flowering tops was also commended for retention of urine and for inflammation of the womb, reflecting the broad wound-herb and febrifuge [fever-reducing] character assigned to this plant across medieval European herbalism.
results.preparation: A decoction or infusion of the fresh or dried leaves and flowering tops was prepared in water or ale [cwrw] and taken by the draught [mouthful], typically warm. For external wounds, the bruised fresh herb or a poultice of the boiled plant was applied directly to the affected part and bound with clean linen. Dosage is not precisely specified in the surviving Welsh redaction, but administration was generally repeated morning and evening until relief was obtained.
